title: What Christchurch could have
dek: Why I mapped a rail network for a city that hasn't had a commuter train since the 1970s.
body:
Christchurch has rebuilt its centre. The stadium, the pools, the library, the convention centre and the hospital are all open again, and on a good day the city feels like it has finally caught its breath. What it still doesn't have is a fast, frequent way to get into that centre without a car.

I didn't set out to make a business case. I set out to understand why something so obvious kept not happening. Passenger rail here has been studied, voted on and promised for years, from Aurecon's assessment in 2014 to ECan's business case vote in 2025 and a commuter trial due in 2027. Every report I read was sensible. None of them showed the track, the land, the people and the buses together, so it was hard to picture what any of it would actually look like.

## Start on the track that exists

So I put it all on one map. The existing infrastructure comes from council, ECan, KiwiRail and LINZ open data. On top of that I drew a plan that could start soon and grow: two lines from Rolleston and Rangiora on KiwiRail's existing track, a peak-hour pilot first, then an all-day service.

The first stage has nine stations. Within 800 metres of a station in stages one and two there are 36,230 residents, which is the number that changed how I thought about it. This isn't a train for some imagined future city. It's for people who already live next to the line.

> This isn't a train for some imagined future city. It's for people who already live next to the line.

## Being honest about the hard parts

The trial's first central stop is Pilgrim Place, and I tried to be straight about what that can and can't do. The atlas measures the walk from there to the Bus Interchange, because if the last few hundred metres are awkward, people won't use it. The alternatives view sketches a trench under Manchester St to a station at Tuam St, a block from the interchange and the stadium. I haven't seen that drawn anywhere else, and I'd love someone who knows more than me to pull it apart.

The numbers behind the story are why I kept going. Greater Christchurch is expected to reach 700,000 people by 2051, up from about half a million. TomTom ranks our rush-hour congestion the worst in New Zealand, at 45.6%, and the average driver loses 89 hours a year in it. By the time the trial starts, it will be 51 years since the last Rangiora commuter train.

## Christchurch as the hub

The project has grown since. It's now the South Island Atlas, with Christchurch at the centre and the history view tracing every South Island branch line, its stations and junctions, 667 stations and stopping places in all. Seeing how connected the island once was makes the gaps today feel less like fate and more like a choice.

I want the atlas to be the start of a public business case: something anyone can open, understand in ten short pages and get a bit excited about. If you work in transport, planning or local government and think I've got something wrong, please tell me. That's exactly the conversation I'm hoping for.
